inputs.original_text: Stable petrol and diesel prices are a distraction, not proof that anyone is protecting consumers. The conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran is being framed as a reason higher oil costs are inevitable, while excise-duty cuts give the government a public-relations cover and quietly drain revenue. With India dependent on crude imports, ordinary people remain exposed—and the same institutions managing the crisis get to shape the story around it. The long-term consequences are being left vague for a reason: keeping people focused on today’s prices makes it easier to hide who benefits and who will pay later.
inputs.modified_text: Don’t mistake steady petrol and diesel prices for protection; they’re the stage dressing. The conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran is being used to make future price rises sound unavoidable, while excise-duty cuts give the government a convenient public-relations shield. The real arrangement is about controlling the story now and deciding later who absorbs the cost. With India reliant on imported crude, ordinary people are left exposed while the institutions managing the crisis also manage what people are told. The vagueness about long-term consequences isn’t an oversight—it keeps attention on today’s prices and away from who benefits when the bill eventually lands.
